evidence: src/orders/presentation/orders.controller.ts: @Controller('orders') and the route decorators (@Post, @Get, @Patch, @Delete, @HttpCode) are transport/framework concerns, which fit the infrastructure layer.
createOrder, addItem, removeItem, changeQuantity, confirmOrder, shipOrder, deliverOrder and cancelOrder each only map request data into a call to an application service's execute().
getOrders and getOrder build GetOrdersQuery/GetOrderQuery and pass them to queryBus.execute. This is delegation only; no query logic lives in the controller.
There are no domain invariants, state-transition checks or repository/database calls anywhere in the file.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrdersController sits in the infrastructure layer, and everything in it is transport work. The NestJS route decorators map HTTP routes. Params, query strings and bodies are pulled out of the request and turned into use-case input objects or CQRS queries, and the work is handed to application services or the QueryBus. The file sets HTTP status codes and shapes the response, as in `createOrder` returning `{ id }`. It contains no business rules: no order state-transition checks, no quantity validation and no pricing. It also contains no persistence logic. That role fits an infrastructure/presentation adapter.
